title: Rounding prices with ROUND
summary: Round converted prices to 2 decimals, whole shillings, tens and hundreds, and see that ROUND changes the stored value.

blocks.text: Head office sends a new price list after a currency conversion. The raw prices have many decimal places, such as KES 1,249.456. Nobody can charge that at the till.

Your job is to round each price in a sensible way: 2 decimals for invoices, whole shillings for shelf tickets and tens for quick budget checks. The ROUND function does this and keeps the sheet correct when prices change.

items: Objective: use ROUND with positive, zero and negative digits.
You pass the mission at 75% or more in the Assessment.

blocks.text: ROUND rounds a number to the number of digits you choose. Digits counts decimal places to the right of the point.
A negative digits value moves to the left of the decimal point. -1 rounds to tens and -2 rounds to hundreds.
Rounds the raw price in B2 to a whole number. Point at the cell instead of typing the price, so the result follows the data.

ROUND changes the value itself. It is not only a change in how the number looks. Example: three lines each cost KES 12.6. The raw total is 37.8. If each price is first rounded with ROUND to 13, the total of the rounded prices is 39.
Tip: halves round away from zero. ROUND(7.5,0) is 8 and ROUND(-7.5,0) is -8. This is the same as Excel's ROUND.
Four questions on ROUND. Type numbers without commas or currency, for example 2400.

items: Positive digits keep decimals, 0 gives a whole number, negative digits round to tens, hundreds and so on.
ROUND changes the stored value, so totals of rounded cells use the rounded numbers.

blocks.text: Next: pricing with ROUND, rounding a discounted price to the nearest KES 10 and finishing with a charm price.

items.prompt: What does a negative digits argument, such as the -1 in =ROUND(B2,-1), do?

options.label: It rounds to tens, hundreds and so on, to the left of the decimal point

items.prompt: B2, B3 and B4 each hold 10.4. C2, C3 and C4 each hold =ROUND(B2,0), =ROUND(B3,0) and =ROUND(B4,0). What does =SUM(C2:C4) return?
